case_name: Bou Malhab c. Diffusion Métromédia CMR Inc.
text:
Unofficial English Translation

Bou Malhab c. Diffusion
Métromédia CMR Inc.

2006 QCCS 2124

SUPERIOR COURT

Canada

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No.:

500-06-000095-998

DATE:

April 20, 2006

______________________________________________________________________

PRESIDING:

THE HONOURABLE

JEAN GUIBAULT, J.C.S.

______________________________________________________________________

FARÈS BOU MALHAB

Claimant

v.

DIFFUSION MÉTROMÉDIA CMR
INC.

and

ANDRÉ ARTHUR

Respondents

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

By judgment dated March 24, 2003, the Court of
Appeal granted the claimant Mr. Farès Bou Malhab leave to proceed with a class
action against the respondents, DIFFUSION MÉTROMÉDIA CMR INC. (Métromédia) and
André Arthur (Mr. Arthur).

[
2
]

This class action involves a claim for moral and
punitive damages for defamation caused, committed, or permitted by the respondents.

[
3
]

The claimant, Mr. Bou Malhab, was approved as
representative plaintiff to bring the class action on behalf of the members of
the class defined by the Court of Appeal, as follows:

[
translation
]

Any person who, on November 17,
1998, was the holder of a taxi driver’s permit in the region of the Island of
Montreal served by urban areas A-5, A-11, and A-12 within the meaning of the
Act
respecting transportation by taxi
, R.S.Q. c. T-11.1, and whose first
language is Arabic or Creole.

[
4
]

In its judgment, the Court of Appeal identified
the main issues to be dealt with collectively and the relevant conclusions as
follows:

[
translation]

A)
THE ISSUES

1.

In November 1998, was André Arthur a servant,
employee, or sub-contractor of the respondent MÉTROMÉDIA CMR MONTRÉAL INC.?

2.

Do the comments of André Arthur and his
listeners, as reproduced, correspond to the comments that were broadcast on the
air on November 17, 1998?

3.

Were the comments of André Arthur and those of
his listener, which André Arthur encouraged or failed to denounce, defamatory
or discriminatory against persons of Arab or Haitian origin who work in the
taxi industry in Montreal, members of the previously defined class?

4.

Are the respondents excused from an action in
defamation by the mere fact that the victims were not specifically named but are
members of a defamed class?

5.

To what amount is each member of the previously
defined class entitled in moral, punitive, and exemplary damages?

B)
THE CONCLUSIONS

1.

ALLOW the class action, with costs;

2.

ORDER the respondents solidarily liable to pay
$750.00 in moral damages and $200.00 in punitive and exemplary
damages to each member of the class.

[
5
]

As instructed by the Court of Appeal, by
judgment dated April 10, 2003, the Honourable Lyse Lemieux, Chief Justice of
the Superior Court at the time, ordered that the class action be brought in the
District of Montreal. The undersigned was named to hear all proceedings in
connection with this action.

THE
FACTS

[
6
]

Around 8:00 a.m. on November 17, 1998, during a
program on Métromédia (CKVL) hosted by Mr. Arthur, allegedly defamatory and racist
comments regarding Arab and Haitian taxi drivers were made.

[
7
]

Mr. Thomassin was appearing as a guest on Mr.
Arthur’s program, and this segment of the show featured a discussion about Quebecers’
satisfaction with restaurants and hotels. On his own initiative, Mr. Arthur added
the Montreal taxi industry to the list of topics.

[
8
]

The comments giving rise to the action against
Mr. Arthur and his employer Métromédia are the following: (cassette D-2 and
verbatim text DM-2)

[
translation]

…

ANDRÉ ARTHUR: … The language …
The
working language in Montreal taxis is Arabic or Creole, and the knowledge of
Montreal is what you might expect. These people
…
Leaving from
Montreal’s Central Station, Place Bonaventure, and going to Verdun, if you
don’t guide the taxi, it can’t get there.

ROBERT
THOMASSIN: Exactly

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: Even though all you have to do is take University, Bonaventure,
Wellington. They can’t do it.
They are all Arabs, they have never gone out
in Montreal
and they’re taxi drivers. I don’t know how they managed to get
a permit!

…

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: …the driver’s exams,
do they work with bribes
?

ROBERT
THOMASSIN: Well, now, I don’t know.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR:
Why is it that there are so many incompetent people and the working
language is Creole or Arabic
in a city that is French and English?

…

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: Is there a listener that can help me understand why Montreal taxis are
so bad? 790-0851.
Why is it that the working language in Montreal taxis is
Arabic and Creole instead of French and English?
Is there someone who can
explain how you become a taxi driver in Montreal?

ROBERT
THOMASSIN: …In the east end, you have a lot of Haitians, there’s no language
problem there, but the rest, it’s the same, y’know.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR:
As long as you speak Creole, because I am not very good at speaking
“nigger”
.

…

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: So I talked about taxis with Thomassin, the very inferior quality of
taxis in Montreal compared to other cities that can be visited. The taxi
situation in Montreal is appalling. There are a few gentlemen we see whose cars
don’t smell bad and aren’t dented and have brakes.

But aside
from that, if you will,
if you don’t speak Arabic or Creole in Montreal
,
you can’t get around in a taxi, you have to avoid taxis,
taxis have become
really, the, the, the Third World of public transport in Montreal
. You
don’t take a taxi in Montreal unless you’re hard up. And if you have a company
and you want to receive clients in Montreal, you don’t tell them: Go to the
airport, then take a taxi. That isn’t done.

You can’t
even get out of a taxi, that, at my place, I do it, you can’t even get out of a
taxi at Central Station and ask to be, to be driven to Verdun. If you don’t
guide the driver, they can’t do it. They are all straight off the boat, people
with no idea.

To me, my
suspicion is that the exams, well, they can be bought
. You can’t have such incompetent people in taxis, people so
ignorant of the city, and believe that these people took real exams. I have to
think, when I see something like that, about bribery.

…

We have some
good calls, Hello, I’m listening.

LISTENER:
Yes, hello, Mr. Arthur.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: Ma’am,

LISTENER:
Yes. I am a taxi driver.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: Yes.

LISTENER:
And there is a course, it costs 700 (500?) dollars apparently, the course for,
for taxis, to follow a course to become a taxi driver. It is given as an
office, the Ligue de taxi de Montréal [Montreal Taxi League].

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: Uh-huh. But then how come …

LISTENER:
But I don’t understand why people go there.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: All right. Is it bribery, ma’am?

LISTENER:
Well, they …

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR:
Why is it that I find myself, why is it that I find myself with
fakirs or Arabs who don’t speak English or French
and who don’t know the
way from Central Station to Verdun?

LISTENER:
Oh, well, I don’t know because they, they all look alike, they must all have
the same pocket number.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: Ah, ah, ah. You think that they share, they share IDs?

LISTENER:
Maybe they share exams too, I don’t know, I don’t understand, because even with
us, they’re aggressive, Arab taxi drivers and all that. They treat us like
dirt.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR:
Yes. Yes. They are very arrogant
.

LISTENER:
Yes. Even with clients, they give clients trouble because …

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: They are arrogant, the taxi drivers in, in Montreal,
the Arabs in
particular are arrogant
, they are often rude, we don’t know at all whether
they are competent and their cars don’t look well-maintained. Why is it like
that, in your opinion?

LISTENER:
Well, I don’t know. They are the ones who always buy the taxis, you know. As
soon as a taxi is sold, it’s an Arab who buys it. They come, they are in, we
are in a minority, we are.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: Why is it that going from downtown to Verdun, the, there are …

LISTENER:
They don’t know the way?

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: Not even four out of five know the way. Four out of five don’t know it.
How did they get their taxi permits?

LISTENER:
Maybe they just give it to them to get rid of them, I don’t know.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: Is it because there is a web of corruption, is it because there are
civil servants who are not doing their job? Is it because they are never
inspected? Why are taxis so dirty in Montreal? Why are they so dented? Why are
they so old? Why are they so badly driven? Why do the brakes screech?

LISTENER:
Why does…

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR:
Why does it smell, why does it smell bad in Montreal taxis?

LISTENER: I
don’t know because I just went through a visual inspection myself last week
because we have visual inspections, and I don’t understand why there are some
taxis that are all dented, that have, that have hardly any more colour, it’s
drab, it’s dingy, and inside, well, anyway, I don’t understand. Do they pay
people?

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: In your opinion, they, can we suspect that there is bribery of the
civil servants who apply it like the, like there was for the parking stickers?

LISTENER:
But I know that when we went for the mechanical inspection, some people have
given money, they put money on the seat, and they passed.

…

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: It’s funny, in a big city, as soon as there’s some, there’s, there’s
garbage, it gets in a taxi. You know, I don’t understand why.

LISTENER: I
think the Arabs are even worse than the blacks.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: We’re not racist, though.

LISTENER:
It’s not a question of racism.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: Of course.

LISTENER:
For me, there are women, old women who we, who are afraid of Arabs because they
get treated badly because they are only going for a three, four dollar trip,
old ladies, sometimes they have trouble walking. They go to the shopping
centre, and it’s four, five bucks, and they get treated badly, they’re called
names.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: Because they, they took…

LISTENER:
Because it was a short trip.

ANDRÉ
ARTHUR: Yes.

LISTENER:
They are afraid, so…

…

[Emphasis
added.]

THE EVIDENCE:

Claim

[
9
]

The claimant, Mr. Bou Malhab, testified as the
main witness. Born in Beirut, Lebanon in 1963, he immigrated to Canada in 1990.
His first language is Arabic, but he attended elementary school in French. When
the program was broadcast on November 17, 1998, he was president of the Ligue
de taxi de Montréal [Montreal Taxi League].

[
10
]

Mr. Bou Malhab first provided the Court with an
explanation of the various mechanisms of the taxi industry in the greater
metropolitan area and described the different governing bodies.

[
11
]

The taxi industry falls under the jurisdiction
of the Bureau du taxi de Montréal [Montreal Taxi Bureau], an institution under
the control of the City, which regulates the entire industry and represents the
interests of its clients. In addition, the Commission des transports du Québec
[Quebec Transit Commission] takes care of permits, while the Société
d’assurance automobile du Québec [Auto Insurance Board of Quebec] controls all
technical aspects of the vehicles and taximeters.

[
12
]

Taxi drivers and owners were grouped under the
Ligue de taxi de Montréal, which has been dissolved and replaced by the
Association professionnelle des chauffeurs de taxi du Québec [Association of
Professional Taxi Drivers of Quebec], which oversees both owners and drivers.

[
13
]

Asked to comment on Mr. Arthur's comments on
CKVL, Mr. Bou Malhab stated that he was deeply injured and humiliated. He
cannot understand why Mr. Arthur singled out Arabs and Haitians for attack. He
said that he was shocked by Mr. Arthur’s suggestion that taxi driver permits
were issued in exchange for bribes. Being a taxi driver in Montreal is not an
easy job, and he finds it particularly unjust for Arabs and Haitians to be
described as incompetent, dirty, and unable to express themselves in French or
English, particularly in Quebec, which defines itself as a welcoming place for newcomers.

[
14
]

He himself speaks Arabic, French, and English,
as well as a little Portuguese. He told the Court that he knows the city well.
Although he is aware of a few taxis in Montreal that are very badly maintained
and driven by arrogant and incompetent drivers, these are exceptions that have
absolutely nothing to do with the two ethnic groups concerned, namely, Arabs
and Haitians.

[
15
]

He obtained a copy of the cassette recording of
Mr. Arthur’s comments, and stated that, when he listened to this cassette with
his colleagues that same day, he had a strong reaction to the comments made by
Mr. Arthur and the listener who telephoned the station during the call-in
segment.

[
16
]

This same cassette was listened to again on
November 27, 1998, at the conclusion of the annual meeting of the Ligue, and on
January 19, 1999, during the board of directors’ meeting. Finally, it was heard
by the Court at the hearing of this case, in the presence of the parties and
counsel.

[
17
]

Mr. Bou Malhab told the Court that a complaint
had been filed with the CRTC but that the complaint had been dismissed. In
cross-examination, he confirmed that he did not believe it was appropriate to
respond to Mr. Arthur’s comments in writing in a newspaper such as La Presse or
The Gazette and that he did not attempt to contact the radio host during his
show on CKVL to contradict the comments made by Mr. Arthur and his listener.

[
18
]

Mr. Bou Malhab concluded his testimony with an
impassioned plea in support of the class action he has undertaken.

[
19
]

The second witness heard by the Court was Mr. El
Helou, taxi owner and driver in Montreal since 1994. Originally from Lebanon,
he speaks fluent Arabic and French, and holds a law degree from the University
of Beirut.

[
20
]

He told the Court that he heard the report live,
while he was working. Because he speaks French fluently, he was hurt by Mr.
Arthur’s remarks regarding the lack of knowledge of the language, as well as by
the suggestions that immigrants are dirty and incompetent. He felt humiliated
by the comments made by Mr. Arthur and his listener on CKVL.

[
21
]

Mr. El Helou arrived in Quebec in 1987, married
a woman from Quebec, and is the father of three children. He feels that these
insults spill over onto his entire family and that they are inexcusable and
imbued with racism.

[
22
]

The third witness, Mr. Azouri, also of Lebanese
origin, studied with the Brothers of the Sacred Heart in Beirut and speaks
fluent French, English, and Arabic. He describes himself as very well integrated
in the Quebec community. After a colleague told him about the program, he
listened to about half of it. He stated that he was hurt and humiliated by Mr.
Arthur’s comments. According to the witness, they were malicious and entirely
gratuitous comments, and he considers them to be completely unacceptable.

[
23
]

The fourth witness was Mr. El Kalaani, who emigrated
from Lebanon in late 1988. He speaks French, English, and Arabic, and has been
a taxi driver in Montreal since 1992. He attended Saint Joseph University in
Beirut, where he received a diploma in business administration.

[
24
]

On the morning of November 17, 1998, while he
was driving a client to a destination, he received a call from a colleague who
told him to listen to the last part of the comments.

[
25
]

He told the Court that he cannot forget the
remarks he heard during Mr. Arthur’s program on CKVL, and that they deeply
humiliated and shocked him. His wife even wants him to change jobs. He was
particularly shocked by the allegations that taxis driven by Arabs are dirty
and smell bad. He cannot understand why Mr. Arthur singled out Arabs and
Haitians in particular.

[
26
]

The fifth witness was Mr. Simon Beaudin.
Originally from Haiti, he has been a taxi driver in Montreal since 1980. He
speaks fluent Creole, French, and English.

[
27
]

On the morning of November 17, 1998, Mr. Beaudin
was in his car when he received a call from a friend telling him that a program
about taxis was about to begin on CKVL. He hurriedly tuned in to the station.

[
28
]

Like the witnesses of Arab origin, he stated
that he was profoundly humiliated and angered by Mr. Arthur’s comments. He
described Mr. Arthur’s comments as dishonest, and considers them to be an incitement
to violence. The expression “nigger", which Mr. Arthur employed, is used
to demean and reject black people and can be defined as racist without the
slightest hesitation. He told the Court that he tries to do his work the best
he can, that he has chosen neither his colour nor his country of origin, and
that such comments caused injury to his entire community and angered him.

[
29
]

The following witness, Mr. El-Samour, is of
Lebanese origin. A taxi driver since 1990, he speaks fluent Arabic, English,
and French.

[
30
]

Like the other witnesses, he experienced Mr.
Arthur’s comments as profound attacks on his dignity. Admittedly, the taxi
industry is not perfect, but he cannot understand why Arabs and Haitians were
singled out. He told the Court that he always outlined the shortest route to
the destination to his clients, and he described his vehicle as clean and always
in good repair.

[
31
]

Mr. El-Samour did not listen to the program on
CKVL live and only heard the cassette later when it was played for him. He
claimed that his work was affected and that he was under more stress. He felt
demeaned and inferior to others, and he described the comments as entirely
unacceptable.

[
32
]

The second witness originally from Haiti was Mr.
Pierre, who has been driving a taxi in Montreal since 1979. He speaks fluent
Creole, French, and English.

[
33
]

He stated that he listened to the program the morning
it was broadcast. He described Mr. Arthur’s comments as extremely malicious,
humiliating, and insulting to Arabs and Haitians. He particularly deplored the
use of the term "nigger", an expression that is seen to be highly
pejorative to Haitians and black people in general.

[
34
]

Mr. Pierre emphasized the fact that his car was
always spotless and mentioned that he had a client in his car during the
program.

[
35
]

The third witness originally from Haiti was Mr.
Max Louis Rosalbert, who has been a taxi driver in Montreal since 1978. He
speaks fluent Creole, French, and English. When the program was broadcast in
November 1998, he was vice-president of the Ligue de taxi de Montréal. He listened
to the program in his office. He described Mr. Arthur’s comments as insulting,
degrading, and humiliating. According to the witness, the
expression “nigger” is revolting, insulting, and unacceptable, and making
a link between “niggers” and the dirtiness of cars was dishonest, to say the
very least.

[
36
]

The following testimony was rendered by Mr. Jean
Kheir, who has been a taxi driver since 1990 and president of the Ligue de taxi
de l’Ouest de Montréal [Taxi League of West Montreal] since 1997.
Mr. Kheir speaks fluent Arabic, French, and English, as well as a little
Spanish.

[
37
]

Originally from Lebanon, Mr. Khier holds an
undergraduate degree in mathematics. He did not listen to the program on the
morning of November 17, 1998 and heard it for the first time when he got
together with other drivers after a meeting. He listened to it again with his
attorney while preparing for trial. He stated that Mr. Arthur’s comments were
false and intolerable to an honest worker. He said that he was hurt by the
comments broadcast on CKVL and he cannot understand why Arabs and Haitians were
singled out. There is no ethnic community that presents any particular problem,
and if there are problems, they are individual and exceptional. It was unjust
to treat Arabs this way, and his entire family has suffered humiliation.

[
38
]

The penultimate witness was Mr. Boudiba, Algerian
in origin, a Canadian citizen since 1983, and a taxi driver since 1984. He
stated that he speaks fluent French, English, and Arabic. Mr. Boudiba did not
hear the program live in November 1998; it was played for him later, at his
attorney’s office. He said he was shocked, hurt, and embarrassed by the radio
host’s comments. He described the connection between Arabs and the dirtiness of
taxis as racist. There was in his opinion no reason to single out Arabs and
Haitians.

[
39
]

The last witness heard on the defamation claim
was Mr. Saba, originally from Lebanon and a taxi driver since 1997. He told the
Court that he had gone to French school in Lebanon and that he speaks fluent
Arabic, English, and French.

[
40
]

He listened to the program with a client in his car,
and he told the Court that his client was particularly embarrassed by the radio
host’s comments calling taxi drivers of Arab origin incompetent, ignorant, and
dirty. The client even felt obliged to apologize to him for these comments.

[
41
]

He stated that he felt attacked by the comments
because the words were degrading and indicated a clear lack of respect for
drivers of Arab or Haitian origin.

[
42
]

In cross-examination, all of the witnesses heard
in support of the claim confirmed that, for one reason or another, they did not
feel it was appropriate to contact the radio station to complain about Mr.
Arthur's remarks or to try to correct or rectify the situation. They all felt
that it would have been completely futile to do so, and the Court shares their
opinion.

[
43
]

All of the witnesses heard in support of the
claim confirmed that they never used Arabic or Creole to converse with third
parties while there were clients in their vehicles, and they all confirmed that
their disciplinary records were clean, that there had never been any complaints
about them, and that they had never been sanctioned.

[
44
]

The final witness heard in the claim was Mr.
André Arthur, a respondent in the present case, to establish the high number of
complaints that have been lodged against him with the Conseil de presse du
Québec [Quebec Press Council] and the CRTC, as well as the numerous civil suits
that have been brought against him for various comments he has made at one time
or another that have been broadcast on radio stations where he was employed as
host.

[
45
]

Reference was made to a specific case involving
another radio host, Mr. Gillet, as well as former premier Daniel Johnson and
his wife,
[1]
which has
received a great deal of media attention.

[
46
]

When questioned, Mr. Arthur denied singling out
the two communities concerned, namely, Arabs and Haitians. He did admit,
however, that approximately forty civil suits have been brought against him
since 1970

Defence

[
47
]

The first witness heard for the defence was Mr.
André Arthur, a journalist and radio host of long standing and experience.

[
48
]

He likened his role on the CKVL morning show to
a straight man who acts as a bridge between the various participants.

[
49
]

Following a discussion of restaurants and hotels
that focussed on Montreal in particular, he moved on to the Montreal taxi
industry, which he described as being profoundly unwell. He decided, among
other things, to talk about his personal experiences, the serious difficulties
he had faced when trying to communicate in English or French with drivers, and
the fact that the drivers were incapable of taking him from Central Station to
his residence in Verdun unless he gave them detailed directions.

[
50
]

He stated that he has been obliged to take long
trips in dirty, foul-smelling, and poorly maintained vehicles, and that he
finds it unsettling when drivers carry on conversations in a foreign language on
the telephone or taxi radio.

[
51
]

He described the taxi industry as the third
world, where the drivers are recent immigrants who know the city a little or
not at all, and obtained their permits because of excessive leniency or through
bribery.

[
52
]

There is no doubt that Mr. Arthur, like the
Court, was very favourably impressed with the quality of the testimony rendered
in support of the claim, and he apologized if he offended or hurt any of these
witnesses.

[
53
]

He told the Court that he had not been targeting
specific ethnic groups such as Arabs or Haitians, but the taxi industry as a
whole. He referred to Arabs and Haitians only because they are the majority. He
was particularly critical of the fact that many taxi drivers use the informal
term of address ("
tu
") with him, and on several occasions he
compared Montreal taxi drivers with New York drivers, whom he considers to be
much more efficient and unquestionably superior.

[
54
]

He deplored the fact that none of the Arab or
Haitian taxi drivers contacted him during the November 17, 1998 program to
share their comments and correct the impression that his remarks may have given
his listeners.

[
55
]

Finally, specific references to Arabs, Creoles, and
fakirs, as well as the use of the expression “nigger” may have been imprudent
but cannot be described as racist. According to the witness, he wished to
address his criticisms to the industry as a whole, with, of course, a certain
emphasis on Arabs and Haitians, since they constitute the majority in the
Montreal taxi industry.

[
56
]

The testimony of both Mr. Arthur and his
accountant touched on his income and his ability to deal with a judgment
against him that ordered exemplary damages, which could be awarded in the present
case.

[
57
]

The two witnesses placed a great deal of
emphasis on the fact that Mr. Arthur’s income has diminished considerably in
recent years, both personally and through the holding company of which he is
the sole shareholder. The court was urged to take this into account as an
important factor when considering whether to order punitive damages.

[
58
]

Ms. Amanda Jelowiicki was also heard as a
witness for the defence. This witness commented upon two reports on the Montreal
taxi industry that she had done for her employer, The Montreal Gazette, in 1998
and 1999. These two reports were extremely interesting because they reveal a
serious problem with the Montreal taxi industry.

[
59
]

Ms. Jelowiicki and her companion identified
themselves as American tourists visiting Montreal. The first article reported
the fact that two-thirds of the drivers they told to go to the Casino drove
right up to the doors of that establishment, even though the Casino was closed
due to a strike and a sign in French indicating the closure was posted at the
access road entrance and had been pointed out to the drivers. The taxi drivers
made a completely useless round-trip to the Casino, even though the
French-language sign confirmed the closure.

[
60
]

For the second report, Ms. Jelowiicki took
approximately $400 worth of taxi rides over three days in Montreal. She
confirmed that her experience was quite negative because many of the cars were
dirty and poorly maintained. There was also a language problem, with some
drivers understanding neither French nor English. She also related the fact
that some drivers had been very unhappy when she took a taxi in front of a
hotel, for example, and asked to be driven to another, not-too-distant location
in the city instead of a location like Dorval, as the driver had hoped.

[
61
]

Finally, she related an incident when the driver
became very angry because she could not provide precise directions to a
location, even though she had already told him that she was a tourist.

[
62
]

These two experiences demonstrate a significant
problem in the taxi industry, at least at the time of these two reports in 1998
and 1999. They have little relevance to the present case, however, since the
dispute is not related to the problems with taxis but to the fact that Mr.
Arthur attributed all such problems to two ethnic groups, Arabs and Haitians.

[
63
]

The last witness heard for the defence was Mr.
Gilles Senécal, who, at the time of the program in November 1998, was director
of human resources and corporate affairs at Métromédia. He simply confirmed to
the Court that Mr. Arthur’s program was a typical morning show, that he had received
only one complaint following the report, namely, the complaint lodged by counsel
for the claimant Mr. Bou Malhab and the Association of which he was president.

[
64
]

Finally, he confirmed that there was no guide or
code of ethics at CKVL at the time of the program at issue, and that there had
been no discussion of the complaints and the civil suits that had been brought
against Mr. Arthur before the station entered into contract P-1A with him.

[
65
]

In his defence, Mr. Arthur also emphasized to
the Court that his feature on the Montreal taxi industry arose from a report
entitled the “Bossé Report”, which outlined taxi problems in the greater
metropolitan area.

[
66
]

The evidence, however, reveals that the “Bossé
Report” was from 1970 and that it had nothing whatsoever to do with the quality
of service. Rather, it addressed the excessive number of taxis in Montreal and
the appropriateness of reducing the number of permits.

ANALYSIS

[
67
]

In its analysis, the Court intends to answer the
questions formulated by the Court of Appeal in its judgment of March 24, 2003.
First question:

[
translation]

In November 1998, was André Arthur
a servant, employee, or sub-contractor of the respondent MÉTROMÉDIA CMR
MONTRÉAL INC.?

[
68
]

This first question presents no particular
problem. The Agreement between MÉTROMÉDIA CMR INC. and ANDRÉ ARTHUR
COMMUNICATIONS INC. and ANDRÉ ARTHUR, dated November 18, 1997 and in force for
a period of 60 months, from January 1, 1998 to December 31, 2002, was filed as
Exhibit P-1A.

[
69
]

In this respect, clauses 7.1 to 7.3 of the
contract, reproduced below, are of particular interest:

[
translation]

7.1       If legal proceedings are brought against the Company or
the Host for any fact, act, or comment made in the context of the Programs
broadcast on CKVL, CKVL will take up the defence of the Company and the Host,
and CKVL hereby promises to indemnify and hold harmless the Company or Host from
any sum that either party may be ordered to pay, be it in capital, interest, or
judicial or extrajudicial costs. Without limiting the generality of the
foregoing, the promise to indemnify noted above
applies to all damages for
which the Company and the Host may be held liable, including pecuniary, moral,
exemplary, or punitive damages.

(emphasis added)

The
Promise to indemnify contained in this section covers all situations and shall
survive the resiliation or cancellation of this contract. Any legal proceeding
or threat of legal proceeding known or instituted before the end of the term of
this agreement shall be subject to this promise to indemnify, even after the
termination or cancellation of this agreement. Any threat of legal proceeding
or legal proceeding known or instituted after the termination or cancellation
of this Agreement shall be covered by this promise to indemnify if said
proceeding is instituted with respect to facts, acts, or comments that took
place while this agreement was in force and were broadcast on CKVL. In
addition, CKVL promises the Host and the Company that it will ensure that, with
respect to any other broadcast of the programs produced for CKVL and broadcast
on other radio stations, those other radio stations provide the same guarantees
of indemnification as those set out in section 7.1.

For the
purposes of this promise to indemnify, the term of this agreement includes any
renewal of this agreement, any tacit renewal, and any period following the term
of this agreement or following the termination or cancellation of this
agreement during which the Company or Host continued to hold a position at CKVL
with or without contractual agreement.

In
addition, the cancellation of this agreement shall not have the effect of
cancelling this indemnification clause, which shall therefore be considered to
be a separate agreement supplemental to this agreement.

7.2

Notwithstanding the provisions in section 7.1,
the
Company and the Host nevertheless agree to reimburse CKVL solidarily, upon
written request to this effect, a sum equal to 25% of the capital amount of any
settlement or payment ordered
in relation to an action contemplated in
section 7.1, up to
a maximum of $50,000
. The sum mentioned shall be
cumulative, and if not used shall continue to be added each year until the end
of the agreement. The capital sum mentioned above shall exclude any interest
and additional compensation provided by the
Civil Code of Québec
for
which CKVL is solely responsibility with, if appropriate, CJMF.

(emphasis added)

7.3

The Company and the Host may elect as
representatives their own counsel and experts, with the agreement of CKVL and
at the expense of CKVL, provided their fees are competitive. In the event that
counsel is not the same as that selected by the Company and the Host, the
Company and the Host shall be released from their obligation to pay the amount
equal to 25% of the capital amount of any settlement or payment order referred
to in section 7.2.

[
70
]

Thus, not only were legal proceedings
specifically contemplated in the contract, Métromédia had also agreed to hold
Mr. Arthur harmless from any claim, including claims for pecuniary, moral,
exemplary, or punitive damages, with the exception of $50,000 per year,
calculated on a cumulative basis, which is to be assumed by Mr. Arthur under
the clause reproduced above.

[
71
]

This is in fact the same contract that was
analyzed in greater detail by Julien J. of the Court of Appeal in
Johnson,
[2]

which upheld joint and solidary liability.

[
72
]

The legal relationship between the two
respondents is clearly established under the terms of this agreement and ultimately,
any liability for a fault committed by the host must be found to be solidary.

[
73
]

The second question as formulated by the Court
of Appeal reads as follows:

[
translation]

Do the comments of André Arthur and
his listeners, as reproduced, correspond to the comments that were broadcast on
the air on November 17, 1998?

[
74
]

An audio cassette and a verbatim transcript of
the comments made during the November 17, 1998 program have been filed as
Exhibits P-3, D-2 and D-AA2. In addition, the Court listened to the cassette
filed as Exhibit P-3 at the hearing and again during deliberations.

[
75
]

This second question was not debated at the
hearing. It is admitted that the comments for which Mr. Arthur is faulted in
the motion to institute proceedings do indeed form part of the remarks made by
Mr. Arthur on CKVL around 8:00 a.m. on November 17, 1998.

[
76
]

The third question posed by the Court of Appeal
is the following:

[
translation]

Were the comments of André Arthur
and those of his listener, which André Arthur encouraged or failed to denounce,
defamatory or discriminatory against persons of Arab or Haitian origin who work
in the taxi industry in Montreal, members of the previously defined class?

[
77
]

This question is at the very heart of the
dispute opposing Mr. Bou Malhab and the respondents Métromédia and André
Arthur. When Mr. Arthur singled out taxi drivers of Arab or Haitian origin on
his November 17, 1998 program, he was probably not thinking of taxi drivers of
the quality of those heard as witnesses at the hearing.

[
78
]

The Court was greatly impressed with the quality
of the testimony offered by the eight witnesses of Arab origin and the three
witnesses of Haitian origin. They expressed themselves in excellent French, and
they all stated that they were perfectly trilingual, speaking both French and
English in addition to their mother tongue. They spoke coherently and with
confidence.

[
79
]

Mr. Arthur may have been justified in
criticizing the taxi industry because many cars are dirty, soiled, and poorly
maintained, because many drivers have little or no familiarity with the city,
because some drivers understand neither English nor French, and because some
are less than honest—to say nothing of those who aggressively display their
annoyance if the trip is not long enough when they were hoping for a fare to
the airport. There was, however, absolutely no reason to single out drivers of
Arab or Haitian origin, as the evidence at the hearing reveals.

[
80
]

Mr. Arthur exhibited racism in singling out
Arabs and Haitians. It was particularly insulting and hurtful to insinuate that
they had obtained their permits illegally and to refer on several occasions to
the use of bribery to obtain a taxi driver’s permit.

[
81
]

The Court can understand why the drivers who
testified in the present case were shocked and hurt by Mr. Arthur’s comments;
these remarks should not have been directed toward people of these two ethnic
groups but toward some drivers, whatever their race.

[
82
]

Indeed, if Mr. Arthur had criticized the taxi
industry in general, without making any reference to drivers of Arab or Haitian
origin, there would have been no problem, since there can be no question that
the quality and services of Montreal taxi drivers are a matter of public
interest.

[
83
]

When he remarked on the listener’s comments and
called her a racist, he was being entirely sarcastic, since both his own comments
and the listener’s had been provoked by his remarks concerning Arabs.

[
84
]

The taxi industry, the subject addressed by Mr.
Arthur on November 17, 1998, was a topic of great interest to the population as
a whole and to the tourist industry in particular. The taxi from the airport or
station is often where tourists to Montreal receive their first impression of
the city, one that can colour their entire stay.

[
85
]

A warm welcome in one of the two official languages
in a well-maintained car will give tourists a positive impression of their
trip, while the opposite situation can be upsetting.

[
86
]

Was it necessary to target Arab and Haitian
drivers to argue his point of view? The Court does not believe so.

[
87
]

There is not a shred of evidence that the taxi
problem in Montreal, if there is one, can be attributed to drivers of Arab and
Haitian origin; on the contrary. Mr. Arthur cannot generalize on the basis of a
few personal experiences and lay the blame for all of the problems discussed in
his program on Arab and Haitian drivers.

[
88
]

When Mr. Arthur used the expression
"nigger”, he ridiculed, vilified, and denigrated the language used by the
large majority of Haitians when they communicate with each other. It is a
particularly pejorative expression, one generally used to demean black people
and poke fun at their mother tongue. When he suggested that Arab and Haitian
drivers pay bribes to get their permits, and when he stated that they do not
know the city and that they drive dirty, foul-smelling, and poorly maintained
cars, he directly attacked their reputation.

[
89
]

The general impression received from listening
to the program is that the problems with Montreal taxis are the fault of Arabs
and Haitians, that they alone are responsible, and that they should receive all
the blame.

[
90
]

Most taxi drivers do a good job, but there are
exceptions. Inasmuch as drivers of Arab and Haitian origin represent the
majority, it may be imagined that such exceptions are more common among drivers
in these two groups. There is no basis, however, for generalizations.

[
91
]

When Marcelin J. and the Court of Appeal ruled
on the application for leave, they described Mr. Arthur’s comments as
unacceptable. In light of the testimonies of the eleven witnesses heard in
support of the claim, the Court finds that these comments are appropriately
defined as defamatory and discriminatory toward taxi drivers of Arab and
Haitian origin working in Montreal.

THE APPLICABLE LAW

[
92
]

There can be no analysis of the defamation,
however, without a consideration of another equally fundamental and important
right, namely, the right to freedom of expression and freedom of the press. As
the Courts have frequently pointed out, it is not always easy to strike the
proper balance between these two rights.

[
93
]

These two rights can easily be exercised
simultaneously, and the right to information may be exercised while respecting
persons. It is always very dangerous to generalize, especially when specific
groups are being targeted.

[
94
]

In
Prud’homme
,
[3]

Lebel J., for the Supreme Court of Canada, clearly established that the
analysis and determination of whether there has been defamatory libel must be
carried out in light of the
Civil Code of Québec
and in harmony with the

Charter of human rights and freedoms
.

[
95
]

Therefore, the law applicable to the present
case is the following:

(1)
Civil Code

3.
Every person is the holder of personality rights, such as the right
to life, the right to the inviolability and integrity of his person, and the
right to the respect of his name, reputation and privacy.

These
rights are inalienable.

RESPECT
OF REPUTATION AND PRIVACY

35.
Every person has a right to the respect of his reputation and
privacy.

No one
may invade the privacy of a person without the consent of the person unless
authorized by law.

CONDITIONS
OF LIABILITY

1.-
General
provisions

1457.
Every person has a duty to abide by the rules of conduct which
lie upon him, according to the circumstance, usage or law, so as not to cause
injury to another.

Where he
is endowed with reason and fails in this duty, he is responsible for any injury
he causes to another person by such fault and is liable to reparation for the
injury, whether it be bodily, moral or material in nature.

He is
also liable, in certain cases, to reparation for injury caused to another by
the act or fault of another person or by the act of things in his custody.

1621.

Where the awarding of punitive damages is
provided for by law, the amount of such damages may not exceed what is
sufficient to fulfil their preventive purpose.

Punitive
damages are assessed in the light of all the appropriate circumstances, in
particular the gravity of the debtor's fault, his patrimonial situation, the
extent of the reparation for which he is already liable to the creditor and,
where such is the case, the fact that the payment of the damages is wholly or
partly assumed by a third person.

Charter of human rights and freedoms
, R.S.Q., c. C-12.

3.
Every person is the possessor of the fundamental freedoms,
including freedom of conscience, freedom of religion, freedom of opinion,
freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association.

4.
Every person has a right to the safeguard of his dignity,
honour and reputation.

5.
Every person has a right to
respect for his private life.

44.
Every person has a right to information to the extent provided by
law.

49.
Any unlawful interference with any right or freedom recognized
by this
Charter
entitles the victim to obtain the cessation of such
interference and compensation for the moral or material prejudice resulting
therefrom.

In case
of unlawful and intentional interference, the tribunal may, in addition,
condemn the person guilty of it to punitive damages.

[
96
]

Defamation is the source of an abundant case law
and a considerable amount of doctrine.

[
97
]

In
Société Radio-Canada

v.

Radio
Sept-Îles inc.
,
[4]

it is specifically defined as follows:

[
translation]

Generically speaking, defamation
consists in the communication of spoken or written remarks that cause someone
to lose in esteem or consideration, or that prompt unfavourable or unpleasant
feelings toward him or her. It implies unlawful interference with a person’s
reputation through negative remarks about the person or the hatred, contempt or
ridicule to which he or she is exposed. (References
omitted.)

[
98
]

Beaudoin and Deslauriers
[5]

tell us the following:

[
translation]

In the civil law, there is no
difference between defamation according to the strict meaning of the word and
defamatory libel as it is known in criminal law. Any injury to reputation, be
it verbal (speech, songs, mimicry) or written (letter, legal proceeding,
caricature, portrait, etc.), public (newspaper or magazine articles, books,
radio or television commentary) or private (letter, pamphlet, report, brief),
whether merely abusive or also defamatory, or whether arising from an
assertion, imputation, or insinuation, constitutes a fault which, if it gives
rise to damage, must be punished by pecuniary compensation. The term defamation
is generally employed in a broad sense to cover insult and verbal abuse, and is
not strictly limited to injury to reputation.

For defamation to give rise to an
action in damages, its author must have committed a fault. This fault may be
the result of two types of conduct. The first is conduct in which the
defendant, knowingly, in bad faith, with the intent to harm, attacks the
reputation of the victim and tries to ridicule or humiliate him or her, or
expose the victim to the hatred or contempt of the public or a group. The
second results from conduct in which there is no intent to harm, but in which
the defendant has nonetheless interfered with the reputation of the victim
through the defendant’s temerity, negligence, impertinence, or carelessness.
Both kinds of conduct constitute a civil fault and entitle the victim to
reparation, and there is no difference between them in terms of right.

[
99
]

In light of the preceding, the Court finds:

1.

That defamation must be assessed as directed by
the Supreme Court, according to the criteria established in the civil law, even
in the case of a class action suit: fault, damage, and causation;

2.

That Mr. Arthur was at fault and caused injury
to the reputation of taxi drivers whose first language is Arabic and Creole,
both directly by declaring that they spoke neither English nor French, that the
vehicles were dirty and poorly maintained, that they smelled bad, and that they
did not know the city, and indirectly by suggesting that there was corruption
and that permits were issued in exchange for bribes, and by inciting a participant
to comment on the same subject and making remarks regarding racism that were,
as the Court has already noted, much more sarcastic than disapproving;

3.

That there was no justification for restricting
his criticism and commentary to taxi drivers whose first language was Arabic or
Creole.

JOINT AND SOLIDARY LIABILITY OF THE DEFENDANTS

[
100
]

It is not necessary to dwell at any great length
on this specific aspect of the case. On April 2, 1998, when called on to
analyze the same contract in light of Mr. Arthur's comments about Daniel
Johnson and Suzanne Marcil (which were made around the same time in a program
broadcast by CKVL
[6]
), Julien J.
concluded that there were grounds to hold the respondents solidarily liable. A
recent judgment of the Court of Appeal has confirmed the decision rendered by
Julien J.
[7]

[
101
]

Métromédia included no caveat in its contract
with Mr. Arthur. Not only did it understand the risk that Mr. Arthur would use inappropriate
language, this was in fact the very reason he was hired to host a very popular
program, in the hopes of drawing higher ratings.

[
102
]

The clauses of the contract with Mr. Arthur,
reproduced above, are most eloquent on this point.

[
103
]

There was no code of ethics at CKVL, and the
numerous complaints and civil suits undertaken against Mr. Arthur had never
been an issue before his program debuted on the radio station.

[
104
]

Métromédia therefore cannot evade solidary
liability for the faults committed by Mr. Arthur.

DAMAGES

[
105
]

It being established that there was defamation
on Mr. Arthur’s part against taxi drivers whose first language is Arabic or
Creole, it falls to the Court to determine whether it is appropriate to award
damages in a class action suit and if so, how much. This task is far from easy.

[
106
]

The action in damages for

defamation
is
essentially an individual remedy
in which the defamed person must establish
that comments made in his or her regard have injured his or her reputation and
have caused a loss of esteem and consideration in the eyes of people he or she
knows.

[
107
]

Is such a remedy incompatible with a claim in a
class action suit, where the defamation affects a group of persons rather than
an individual?

[
108
]

The evidence shows that in 1998, there were
between 1,100 and 1,200 taxi drivers in Montreal whose first language was
either Arabic or Creole.

[
109
]

The fourth question posed by the Court of Appeal
in its judgment of March 24, 2003, reads as follows:

[
translation]

Are
the respondents excused from an action in defamation by the mere fact that the victims
were not named but are members of a defamed class?

(a)
Trial Judgement on the Motion
for Certification

[
110
]

The motion for leave to institute the class
action was heard at first instance by Madam Justice Diane Marcelin.

[
111
]

In her judgment of June 22, 2001,
[8]

she dismissed the motion for leave to bring a class action. In her reasons, she
stated the following:

[
translation]

Aside from the difficulty, if not
the impossibility, of establishing a causal relationship between the report and
the moral damage suffered by an individual when the comments are addressed to a
community with a large number of members, it must be noted that neither Quebec
scholars nor the common law or civil law courts recognize civil remedies for
defamation of a community if the allegations do not target a particular member.
It must be remembered that each plaintiff must prove that the attacks
apparently directed against the particular group actually spill over onto that
plaintiff on particular.

As already mentioned, however, the
larger the group, the more diffused the attack; the more it affects the
community, the less it is felt by the individual.

(b)
Court of Appeal Decision on Leave to Bring a
Class Action

[
112
]

As noted above, on March 24, 2003, the Court of Appeal overturned
the judgment of Marcelin J., allowed the motion, and granted leave to bring a
class action.

[
113
]

To the following question:

[
translation]

Can one thousand taxi drivers bring
a claim in defamation in a class action?

[
114
]

Rayle J. for the Court of Appeal answered “Yes".

[
115
]

In paragraphs 42 to 44 of her decision, Madam
Justice Rayle wrote the following:

[
translation]

[42]       The
trial judge concluded that it would be impossible to establish a causal
relationship between the report and the moral damage suffered by an individual
because the disparaging remarks were addressed to a community with a large
number of members. She concludes that in such a case, our law does not
recognize civil remedies for defamation of a community because the attack is
diluted to the point of losing all its power before it spills over onto the
individual.

[43]       With great respect, I do
not share this opinion. An individual can suffer prejudice in a variety of
ways. The person who made the disparaging remarks may achieve such a result by
camouflaging the attack on a particular target in generalizations. This is the
example provided by the author Denis Buron,
supra
. It was also the case
in
Raymond

v.

Abel

(1946) C.S. 251
, in which the defendant
stated on the church steps that all Raymonds (in the parish) were [
translation]
“bastards”.

[44]       The individual
experience may result from the relatively limited size of the targeted group
juxtaposed with the double-pronged nature of the attacks: the specific group
targeted, on the one hand, and the specific insults uttered on the other. The
appellant has serious grounds showing that that is precisely the case here. In
order to feel personally accused of uncleanliness, incompetence, and
corruption, it is sufficient for the Montreal taxi driver to be Haitian or
Arab. Conversely, any Haitian or Arab taxi driver who was operating a taxi on
November 17, 1998 in Montreal is necessarily unclean, incompetent, and corrupt.
André Arthur’s comments allowed no exception. There is a perfect correlation
between these races and the faults he attributes to them. If a worker is of one
of these races, he cannot escape being tarnished in the public opinion and
injured in the most personal aspects of his identity.

[
116
]

In paragraph 47 and following of her judgment,
Rayle J. cited with approval the decision of the Court of Appeal in
Ortenberg
v.

Plamondon
, a case from 1915 where the Court of Appeal recognized
that a Jewish person living in Quebec City, where there were 75 Jewish families
out of a total population of 80,000 people, could claim damages for defamation
because of the degrading and clearly racist comments against Jews made by a
speaker during his lecture.

[
117
]

In light of
Ortenberg
, Rayle J. added:

[
translation]

[50]       From the decision of the
Court of Appeal in
Ortenberg
, we understand that there are three
possible situations in cases involving the defamation of a group:

1-

Collective defamation
targets a large group and gets lost in the crowd. The members are not entitled
to compensation.

2-

There is collective
defamation, but some members are named or easily identifiable. In this case,
the targeted members are entitled to compensation.

3-

The collective
defamation targets a group that is sufficiently limited for all the members to
be personally injured. The members are therefore entitled to damages.

[
118
]

And she concludes in the following manner:

[
translation]

[51]       It is for the court to
determine the extent to which the individual nature of the injury to reputation
is diminished or even eradicated altogether by the size of the community
targeted, by taking into consideration the nature of the comments made and the
circumstances in which the defamation took place. Every case turns on its own
facts. In the first hypothetical situation, the court may determine that the
claim is inadmissible because of a lack of interest and causation, and dismiss
it summarily. In the other cases, it is for the trier of fact to rule on the
merits of the action based on the evidence admitted.

[
119
]

This is how the Court of Appeal concluded that
Mr. Arthur’s comments were
prima facie
defamatory and that 1,000 taxi
drivers whose first language was Arabic or Creole could exercise their right to
damages through a class action suit.

[
120
]

It should be noted that the decision in
Ortenberg,
supra,
was very different from the case before us. In that case there was
one individual claiming damage for himself, not a group or a community; in the
case before us, Mr. Bou Malhab acts on behalf of a considerable number of
individuals, namely, between 1,100 and 1,200 taxi drivers.

[
121
]

In the conclusions of the motion to institute
proceedings, Mr. Bou Malhab claimed from the respondents solidarily $750 in
moral damages for each taxi driver whose first language is Arabic or Creole,
and $200 as punitive and exemplary damages, the whole with interest, including
additional interest.

[
122
]

Eight taxi drivers whose first language is
Arabic, including the plaintiff Mr. Bou Malhab, and three taxi drivers whose first
language is Creole have told the Court that they listened to either Mr.
Arthur’s program or the cassette recording of the program and were profoundly
hurt and shocked by Mr. Arthur’s remarks.

[
123
]

The evidence reveals that there were also at
least ten persons who listened to the cassette after the annual general meeting
of the members of the Ligue de taxi de Montréal, which was held on November 24,
1998.

[
124
]

Thus, of the 1,200 taxi drivers whose first
language is Arabic or Creole, the evidence reveals that at most twenty drivers
heard the program on November 17, 1998 or were able to listen to the cassette
recording of the impugned excerpts.

[
125
]

What about the other 1,180 drivers? How many
listened to the program on November 17, 1998? Or how many were able to listen
to the cassette recording of the program afterwards?

[
126
]

Can a taxi driver whose first language is Arabic
or Creole claim to have suffered damage when he or she never heard Mr. Arthur's
remarks? Can we rely only on the testimony given at the hearing of this case to
infer that there was general knowledge on the part of all Arab or Haitian
drivers that would allow individual damages to be awarded? Is it sufficient to
establish that, on November 17, 1998, a given person was a taxi driver whose
first language was Arabic or Creole for that person to be entitled to damages?

[
127
]

How big was the audience of CKVL, a
French-language radio station, on November 17, 1998?

[
128
]

All the witnesses heard by the Court at the
hearing have French as a second language.

[
129
]

How many taxi drivers with Arabic or Creole as
their first language and English as their second language listened to Mr.
Arthur’s comments or even heard about them?

[
130
]

Must we draw a distinction between “francophones”
and “anglophones”?

[
131
]

These are extremely important questions, and their
answers are far from obvious.

[
132
]

In the view of the Court, a taxi driver may
claim damages only if it can be established that he or she heard Mr. Arthur’s
comments during the program or afterwards. This is the case for the 11
witnesses who testified at the hearing. As for the others, there is no evidence
whatsoever indicating that they are even aware of the content of Mr. Arthur's
program on CKVL on November 17, 1998.

[
133
]

Can this deficiency be compensated for in a
class action suit, where each individual presents his or her own claim? The
court does not believe so, since there is absolutely no way of verifying each
and every statement that could be made by any one of the taxi drivers concerned.

[
134
]

Indeed, it is easy to establish that an
individual was a taxi driver in Montreal on November 17, 1998 and that his or
her language is Arabic or Creole, but it is absolutely impossible to verify whether
he or she listened to the program or heard the cassette on the date he or she
claims. A mere sworn statement that a person has done so it would be
insufficient.

[
135
]

When the Court of Appeal allowed the application
for leave to bring a class action, there is no doubt that it was aware of the
potential problem of proof of individual damage, but it granted leave anyway.
In the Court of Appeal judgment, Rayle J., for the Court, stated the following:

[
translation]

[60] It cannot be denied that the procedural vehicle chosen by the
appellant, who proceeds with the benefit of his community in mind, is
ill-suited
to the exercise of an action in defamation, which is essentially an individual
remedy
.

(Emphasis added.)

[
136
]

In the preceding paragraph, she had stated:

[
translation]

It is for the court to determine the
extent to which the individual nature of the injury to reputation is diminished
or even eradicated altogether by the size of the community targeted, by taking
into consideration the nature of the comments made and the circumstances in
which the defamation took place.

[
137
]

Despite these difficulties, the Court of Appeal
concluded that there was
prima

facie
defamation and that a class
action suit was appropriate. This Court, although it shares the opinion of
Marcelin J., considers itself bound by the Court of Appeal judgment.

[
138
]

Emphasizing the fact that an action in defamation
is essentially an individual remedy, the Court of Appeal for Ontario denied the
class action of the
Seafarers International Union of Canada et al.,
[9]

and the Ontario Court of Justice denied the class action in
Kenora
(Town) Police Service,
[10]

Gauthier

v.

Toronto Star Daily Newspapers Ltd.,
[11]

and
Campbell
v.
Toronto Star Newspaper Ltd.
[12]

[
139
]

Elliott v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp. et al
.
[13]
also deals
with the same subject matter, citing with approval English law to the same
effect.

[
140
]

The difficulty of awarding damages in this case
does not arise from the size of the group targeted, but from the total lack of
evidence of damage suffered by all the taxi drivers concerned that were not
called as witnesses at the hearing.

[
141
]

As we have seen, in
Ortenberg
,
supra
,
the Court of Appeal recognized that
an individual
was entitled to
damages for defamatory statements about a community, since it was established
in that case that the specific claimant had been injured and shocked by the
comments about Jews.

[
142
]

As Lesage J. wrote in
Curateur public

v.

Syndicat National des employés de l’hôpital St-Ferdinand
at 370
:
[14]

[
translation]

At the basis of a class action, there
is a presumption of similarity in favour of the absent members. The plaintiff
must prove it, but he or she is not required to establish each individual
situation. The Court is asked to proceed by groups, and any refusal to do so
would constitute a denial of justice. Whether or not we agree, the legislator
intended the Court to play a new role in the exercise of collective justice.
This role translates into controlling the remedy, controlling proceedings, exercising
discretion with regard to the solutions and method of enforcement, holding the trial
in stages and, above all, adopting an overall approach to the dispute by
treating individual reports collectively, either in whole or in part.

and on page
396 :

[
translation]

The legislator intended the
judicial treatment of the interests of a group of members who share affinities
to be collective. This comprehensive justice offsets the lack of power to
obtain relief through individual action either because of the complexity or
fluidity of the law or because the interests of the class members have been
diluted. This form of remedy assigns the judicial power a new role in defining
an accessible, realistic, uniform, and curative justice, one in which the right
exists but where the sanction would be virtually non-existent otherwise.

In
L’autorisation
d’exercer le recours collectif,
(1980) 21 C. de D.

880-881
,
Mario Bouchard writes:

[
translation]

First, as we have
already noted, class actions make it practical to exercise theoretical rights
by collectivizing the determination of the rights of a group of individuals. It
thus lowers the monetary threshold beyond which action is more profitable than
non-action, and does away with embarrassment, fear, or ignorance as factors
behind the failure to exercise a right. Increasing the effects of a person’s
actions makes these actions all the more profitable and reconciles the
adversarial system, which is left to the initiative of the parties, with the
need to find solutions for “meta-individual” social evils. This increased
judicial effectiveness should also make it possible to prevent too great a
disillusionment on the part of citizens with the judicial system and, for some,
makes the class action the final defence against the juridical paternalism of
the State. This procedural method makes our judicial system compatible with our
model of mass economy.

As we
have also noted, the class action is not intended to be a purely compensatory
solution. Articles 1034 and 1036 C.C.P. authorize the awarding of the undistributed
balance to a third party, if appropriate, “taking particular account of the interest
of the members”. Such a solution, however, need not render the debtor’s
liability more onerous.

These
provisions authorize us to presumptively establish the quantum of the
defendants' liability. When all of the members of the group have suffered the
same type of prejudice, this prejudice may be assessed according to an average,
without increasing the debtor’s liability.

[
143
]

In the present case, only 11 individuals have
stated that they were spoken of in a defamatory manner. The evidence of moral
damages on their part leaves no doubt, and even though there is a presumption
of similarity in favour of the members, as Lesage J. points out, the principles
of civil liability are still relevant and the link between fault and damage
must be established.

[
144
]

Can the Court allow the class action for these
11 individuals only? Or for 21 individuals, to include those who heard Mr.
Arthur’s comments when they listened to the cassette recording of Mr. Arthur’s
comments on his program at the end of the annual meeting in November 1998?

[
145
]

The Court cannot consider such an approach without
subverting the class action. The legislator put this remedy in place precisely
to allow an individual to claim damages on behalf of a group, and for these damages
to then be awarded to each member of that group, provided that each member is
able to establish that he or she suffered the damage. For the reasons outlined
above, this cannot be done in the present case.

[
146
]

In the action presented by Mr. Bou Malhab, the
Court is unable to find a link between the fault and the individual damage to
the taxi drivers concerned, in terms of both moral and, if appropriate,
punitive damages. This approach must therefore be set aside.

[
147
]

Having concluded that Mr. Arthur's comments on
his program on November 17, 1998 were indeed defamatory, but being unable to
award moral or punitive damages on an individual basis, the Court intends to
follow the suggestion of Mr. Bou Malhab in his alternative conclusions and to
take a collective approach to the unclaimed amounts pursuant to articles 1028
and 1034 C.C.P., which provide the following:

1028. Every final judgment
condemning to damages or to the reimbursement of an amount of money orders that
the claims of the members be recovered collectively or be the object of individual
claims.

1034. The court may, if of
opinion that the liquidation of individual claims or the distribution of an
amount to each of the members is impossible or too expensive, refuse to proceed
with it and provide for the distribution of the balance of the amounts
recovered collectively after collocating the law costs and the fees of the
representative's attorney.

[
148
]

In his conclusions, Mr. Bou Malhab suggests in
the alternative that the any remaining unclaimed amount be awarded to a
foundation or a non-profit organization to be named by the Court.

[
149
]

Such an approach is not new to the courts, and
has been used,
inter

alia
, in cases where the amount awarded was
insufficient to constitute an individual claim or when a part of the amounts
awarded by the court remained unclaimed.

[
150
]

Submissions on this aspect of the case were made
by counsel for Mr. Bou Malhab at the hearing and in a letter addressed to the
court and dated December 15, 2005. After discussion with his client, Mr. El
Masri proposes the Association professionnelle des chauffeurs de taxi–exécutif
régional de Montréal [Association of Professional Taxi Drivers of
Quebec–Montreal Regional Executive], as the non-profit organization to be named
by the Court. It appears that there is no non-profit organization that answers
precisely to the definition set out by the Court of Appeal.

[
151
]

In the absence of an organization established to
help, support, and assist taxi drivers whose first language is Arabic or
Creole, the Court expects that it will most likely accept the claimant’s
suggestion and name the Association to collect the amount of damages awarded
below.

[
152
]

Following this judgment, the Court intends to
hear the submissions of this organization regarding the establishment of
support programs aimed at taxi drivers whose first language is Arabic and
Creole and their families. These submissions will be followed by a specific
order regarding the final destination of the amount awarded and the use of the
amounts received. In the event of inadequate submissions, the Court shall make
an
ex parte
ruling on the permitted uses of the sums paid and their
ultimate destination.

[
153
]

The fifth question formulated by the Court of
Appeal is the following:

[
translation]

To what amount is each member of
the previously defined class entitled in moral, punitive, and exemplary
damages?

DAMAGES

1.
Moral Damages

[
154
]

Mr. Bou Malhab claims $750 in moral damages per
taxi driver concerned. For the reasons outlined above, it is not easy for the
Court to determine the moral damages to be awarded in this class action suit to
the non-profit organization that would represent adequate compensation for Mr.
Arthur’s comments. Other courts have found that one dollar per individual is
appropriate when the assessment is for all intents and purposes impossible.
This Court, however, feels that this amount would be altogether inadequate,
while the amount of $750, as suggested in the motion to institute proceedings,
appears excessive and unrealistic.

[
155
]

Since the number of taxi drivers whose first
language is Arabic or Creole who were working in Montreal on November 17, 1998
has not been precisely established, the Court finds that, for the purposes of
establishing the number of persons concerned, there were 1,100 taxi drivers.

[
156
]

As compensation, the Court fixes an amount equivalent
to $200 for each of the drivers and awards a total of $220,000 in moral
damages.

2.
Punitive and Exemplary
Damages

[
157
]

Mr. Bou Malhab claims $200 in punitive damages
per each member of the group. Article 49, paragraph 2 of the
Charter of
human rights and freedoms
stipulates the following:

In case of unlawful and intentional
interference, the tribunal may, in addition, condemn the person guilty of it to
punitive damages.

[
158
]

For its part, the
Civil Code
provides the
following in
article 1621
:

Where the awarding of punitive
damages is provided for by law, the amount of such damages may not exceed what
is sufficient to fulfil their preventive purpose.

Punitive damages are assessed in
the light of all the appropriate circumstances, in particular the gravity of the
debtor's fault, his patrimonial situation, the extent of the reparation for
which he is already liable to the creditor and, where such is the case, the
fact that the payment of the damages is wholly or partly assumed by a third
person.

[
159
]

Insofar as the past foretells the future, when
the contract with Métromédia was entered into, Mr. Arthur’s blunders were not
only foreseeable, they were specifically foreseen. They are subject to a
special clause in which Métromédia agrees to hold Mr. Arthur harmless of any
order to pay, with the exception of $50,000.

[
160
]

Must we therefore conclude that it is
appropriate to award exemplary damages in the circumstances? Does this
constitute an unlawful and intentional interference justifying punitive and
exemplary damages?

[
161
]

The Court does not believe so.

[
162
]

An attentive listening of the cassette and the
testimony of Mr. Arthur, who said that he regrets his words and that he
apologizes to the persons concerned, does not lead us to conclude that there
was unlawful and intentional interference within the meaning of section 49.2 of
the
Charter
.

[
163
]

The Court must place Mr. Arthur's comments in
their very specific context, a morning show where listeners were asked to call
in to comment and share their own experiences.

[
164
]

The topic of the day, the taxi industry in
Montreal, was very interesting. As the Court has already pointed out, had there
been no connection made between the problems and the two specific groups, Arabs
and Haitians, the problems discussed were relevant and perfectly appropriate to
a public affairs program.

[
165
]

In such a context, the Court cannot accept the
claimant’s arguments urging that punitive and exemplary damages be added to the
moral damages.

JUDICIAL AND EXTRAJUDICIAL FEES

[
166
]

At the end of the hearing, counsel for the
claimant filed the professional fees agreement with the claimant as Exhibit
P-19.

[
167
]

This agreement covers both judicial and
extrajudicial fees, the whole within a lawyer-client relationship.

[
168
]

Because the Court in this case has concluded
that it was not appropriate to award punitive and exemplary damages, and
because the awarding of damages as compensation for extrajudicial fees is
subject to the same legal principles, it is not appropriate to award or, in
this case, even to consider awarding damages as reimbursement for extrajudicial
fees.

[
169
]

The agreement filed in the record as Exhibit
P-19 is therefore not relevant, and the fees and expenditures shall be governed
by article 1050.1 C.C.P.

[
170
]

The action is therefore allowed, with costs, in
compliance with said article, and it falls to the claimant and his counsel to
determine whether it is appropriate to present a motion for special fees, as
provided for in the tariff.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
171
]

ALLOWS
the class
action;

[
172
]

OFFICIALLY CERTIFIES
the claimant’s publication of a notice to the members, as ordered in
the judgment of the Court of Appeal

on

March 24,
2003;

[
173
]

ESTABLISHES
, for
the purposes of this judgment, the number of taxi drivers whose first language
was Arabic or Creole to be 1,100;

[
174
]

ORDERS
the
respondents DIFFUSION MÉTROMÉDIA CMR INC. and André Arthur solidarily to pay
the non-profit organization known under the name the Association
professionnelle des chauffeurs de taxi – exécutif régional de Montréal, or any
other non-profit organization that may be designated by the Court, the sum of
$220,000 for all of the taxi drivers whose first language is Arabic or Creole
and who had a permit to drive a taxi in Montreal on November 17, 1998;

[
175
]

ORDERS
the
Association professionnelle des chauffeurs de taxi – exécutif de Montréal to appear
before the undersigned at a date to be determined by agreement between the
counsel of record but no later than 60 days from the date of this judgment in
order to determine the parameters according to which the sums paid to this
organization will be used for taxi drivers whose first language is Arabic or
Creole. The Court reserves the right to designate any other non-profit
organization as it deems appropriate;

[
176
]

SUSPENDS
the
execution and payment of the sum of $220,000 until an order is rendered regarding
the ultimate recipient of the sum thus awarded and the manner of disposing of
that sum;

[
177
]

THE WHOLE
with
interest as of the date of service of the motion to institute proceedings,
including additional indemnity as provided by law,
with
costs
.
